did_you_know.text: Did you know? Hosea compares Israel’s joy to the joy of the nations, but immediately explains that it is undeserved because Israel has prostituted itself by turning away from its God and has loved the payment received on every threshing floor.

Did you know? The chapter describes a time when the threshing floor and winepress will not provide Israel with food and wine; its agricultural produce, which normally symbolizes blessing, will not protect it.
Did you know? The punishment includes exile: Israel will not remain in the Lord’s land, and Ephraim will return to Egypt or eat unclean food in Assyria.

Did you know? The sacrifices Israel offers will not be acceptable to the Lord. They are described as mourning bread—bread associated with grief—which defiles those who eat it and cannot be brought into the house of the Lord.
Did you know? Hosea asks how Israel will be able to celebrate the festival day and the Lord’s feast when sin and disaster stand before it.

Did you know? The chapter announces that the days of punishment and recompense have come, and portrays the prophet as someone Israel may regard as a fool or madman instead of listening to his warning.
Did you know? Israel’s sins are compared with the days of Gibeah, and so it is said that the Lord will remember their guilt and punish their sins.

Did you know? The Lord describes Israel at the beginning of its history as grapes in the wilderness and as the first fruit on a fig tree, but recalls how Israel joined itself to Baal of Peor and became detestable in the Lord’s sight.
Did you know? Ephraim’s glory is described as flying away like a bird—from birth, from the womb, and from pregnancy—a picture emphasizing the loss of its future and continuity.
Did you know? The chapter concludes by describing Ephraim as one who did not listen to the Lord; therefore, God will reject him and make him wander among the nations.
